newsitem.title: GERMANY: Krupp, Thyssen go for steel merger.
newsitem.headline: Krupp, Thyssen go for steel merger.

text.p: Germany's Krupp group called off its dramatic hostile takeover bid for Thyssen AG on Monday, as both companies said they would found a steel joint venture and explore expanding co-operation into other areas.
"The previously announced takeover bid is void and no further offers to take over Thyssen will be made in future," Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp said in a statement jointly issued with Thyssen.

After five-day talks, the two sides agreed to fuse their steel units into a joint venture where Thyssen Stahl would take management control because it has greater capacity and is more profitable than Krupp-Hoesch Stahl, a Thyssen spokesman said.

The two-paragraph joint statement also said: "Negotiations between Thyssen and Krupp over a merger of steel operations are going well. The participants agree that such a merger would enable Germany to survive as a steel production centre and make possible a strategy to move forward."

The two sides have been in talks since Thursday over steel co-operation after Krupp suspended its cash bid which valued Thyssen at 435 marks ($257) a share, a 25 percent premium to the market when it was made at the beginning of last week.
Krupp said its decision to drop its hostile bid for Thyssen did not herald a friendly merger, but there was scope for joint ventures outside the steel production area.
"This does not mean there will be a merger between the two groups," a company spokesman said.
A steel merger would create a venture with capacity of 18 million tonnes a year, making it one of the largest in the world and possibly Europe's biggest.
Share traders and analysts said that Thyssen shares, pumped up by takeover speculation, could fall back on Tuesday but they were unlikely to take a beating.

"Obviously if there is any reaction, it would probably be downward, but I don't expect it will be dramatic," said Andreas Heine, analyst at Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechsel-Bank. He said the agreement was positive for both Thyssen and Krupp.

Shares in the two firms were among the biggest gainers in Monday afternoon trade with Krupp ending up 17.50 marks, or 5.48 percent, at 337 marks, and Thyssen ending the day up 20 marks, or 5.12 percent, at 410.50 marks.

"Logically the Thyssen share price should fall through 400 marks tomorrow, but if they go ahead with some kind of joint venture and include a restructuring, then the market will probably like that," one share trader said.

Heine noted that Thyssen shares were already well below the 435 mark offer price mentioned in Krupp's aborted takeover offer. He has had a "buy" recommendation on Thyssen since late January and has no immediate plans to change that view.

"The takeover scenario was being more and more discounted as time went on. I think that by today some kind of joint venture was seen as the most likely outcome. Krupp and Thyssen have already proved they can cooperate together and now the regular steel activities will come as well," he told Reuters.

Thyssen had earlier said that it would not be possible for Krupp to finance its hostile bid, which valued Thyssen at 13.6 billion marks, without taking irresponsible risks and damaging the interests of shareholders.

Thyssen said 25 percent of its shareholders had indicated they would reject the hostile bid. It said Krupp wanted to buy only 60 percent, leaving minority shareholders owning a piece of a debt-ridden company which would have to slash dividends.

"This high financial risk, compounded by the cyclical steel market, cannot be in the interest of shareholders," the company said. "For an internationally active business such a financial structure bears unjustifiable risks for all concerned."

The Thyssen spokesman said after the joint announcement that the steel venture would offer "the best concept" for its workers and shareholders. "Now we have the time and calm to work out the details," he said.

Despite news of the breakthrough, workers leaders said a demonstration organised by the IG Metall union against the banks behind the defunct Krupp bid would still go ahead in Frankfurt, Germany's financial capital, on Tuesday.

"We have achieved a partial success, but we are going to demonstrate all the same," Georg Bongen, the head of Thyssen's workers' council, told Reuters. Workers fear that up to 7,000 jobs could be lost through through cost-cutting measures.

Some 30,000 workers are expected to descend on Frankfurt to protest near the twin-towered headquarters of Deutsche Bank AG, which with Dresdner Bank AG and U.S. bank Goldman Sachs put together backing for the Krupp bid.
($ = 1.691 German Marks)
